sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
With the increasing penetration of renewable energy such as wind power in power
systems, the proportion of traditional synchronous generators continues to decline, leading
to a significant reduction in system equivalent inertia and increasingly prominent frequency
stability issues [1,2]. Existing studies have shown that high penetration of renewable energy
weakens system inertia support, making the system more prone to higher rates of change of
frequency, lower frequency nadirs, and reduced frequency recovery capability under active
power disturbances, thereby posing serious challenges to secure and stable power system
operation [3–5]. To adapt to the operational requirements of low-inertia power systems,
increasing research attention has been devoted to control methods enabling renewable
energy units, especially wind turbines, to participate in system frequency support [6,7].
Currently, wind turbines mainly participate in grid frequency regulation through
supplementary active-power control strategies. Existing methods can generally be classified
into two categories according to the source of frequency-support energy and the associated
control mechanism: one is frequency-support control based on the release of rotor kinetic
energy, and the other is power-reserve control based on de-loaded operation to maintain
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 4476 https://doi.org/10.3390/app16094476
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 4476 2 of 31
a power margin [8]. The former typically releases rotor kinetic energy in the initial stage
of a sudden system frequency change through supplementary inertia response, virtual
inertia control, or fast power regulation based on the rate of change of frequency (ROCOF),
thereby improving the ROCOF and elevating the frequency nadir. Its advantages include a
fast response speed, making it suitable for the rapid support needs of low-inertia systems,
but it may also induce secondary power fluctuations during the rotor speed recovery phase.
The latter continuously provides active power support after a frequency deviation occurs,
typically through deloaded operation, reserving power margin, or coordination with energy
storage. Its advantages are a longer support duration and relatively stable control, but
it often requires sacrificing partial wind energy utilization efficiency. Extensive research
has been conducted on both types of methods. Ref. [ 9] advanced from fixed-parameter
control to multi-objective adaptive combined inertia-droop control, to enhance frequency
response performance and improve the recovery characteristics of the unit. Ref. [ 10]
proposes a closed-loop synthetic inertia control strategy for wind turbines combined
with over-speeding de-loaded operation, which uses detected frequency deviation as a
feedback signal, to reduce power imbalance during frequency regulation, and effectively
decreases the maximum frequency deviation of the system. Overall, existing studies
primarily evaluate the effectiveness of wind turbine frequency regulation control from the
perspective of enhancing frequency response performance.
However, the participation of wind turbines in frequency regulation is not without
associated costs. During frequency support, the unit must rapidly adjust its active power
output in response to the system frequency deviation and the rate of change of frequency
(ROCOF). These second-level power adjustments substantially exacerbate dynamic oscilla-
tions in key load paths, including drivetrain torque and tower fore–aft bending moments,
thereby accelerating the fatigue damage accumulation of key components [ 11–14]. To
address the structural fatigue issues arising from wind turbine participation in frequency
regulation, research has been initiated to explore strategies such as auxiliary control op-
timization, mechanistic analysis of inertia control, and coordinated frequency support
with energy storage systems [15–18]. Relevant research indicates that frequency support
provided by wind turbines is often accompanied by structural fatigue costs. Suppressing
fatigue damage while ensuring frequency regulation performance has become a critical
issue in research on wind power frequency support.
At present, investigations into the coupled problem of frequency response and fatigue
loads are predominantly conducted using high-fidelity aeroelastic simulation tools such as
OpenFAST (v3.5.0) and Bladed (v4.8). In contrast to analytical approaches that focus exclu-
sively on electrical power responses or utilize low-order simplified models, high-fidelity
co-simulation platforms are capable of simultaneously capturing the multiphysics cou-
pling characteristics across the aerodynamic, structural, drivetrain, and control subsystems.
Consequently, they are better suited for the high-fidelity evaluation of critical fatigue load
channels under diverse operating scenarios. Within this framework, OpenFAST—an open-
source, high-fidelity aeroelastic simulation suite—boasts distinct advantages, including
comprehensive modeling capabilities, robust modular coupling, and the precise characteri-
zation of dynamic responses for blades, towers, and drivetrain components. Accordingly,
it has been extensively utilized in the domains of wind turbine load analysis and control
strategy research. Nevertheless, they suffer from high modeling complexity, long simula-
tion times, and substantial computational cost [ 19]. When frequency regulation control
parameters require repeated evaluation across various disturbance levels, wind speeds,
and parameter combinations, relying solely on high-fidelity co-simulation makes it difficult
to meet the demands of rapid analysis and optimization.
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16094476
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 4476 3 of 31
By comparison, machine learning approaches offer novel insights into the rapid
assessment of structural fatigue loads in wind turbines. In recent years, relevant studies
have made substantial progress in the rapid modeling of wind turbine fatigue response.
Ref. [20] established a data-driven surrogate model that maps wind input time series to
DEL, which can replace some time-consuming aeroelastic simulations with high accuracy.
Subsequent studies further combined SCADA measurements with open-source model data,
utilizing Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to achieve rapid DEL assessment for operating
wind turbines [ 21]. Ref. [ 22] used neural networks to surrogate the rainflow-counting
process, achieving near-real-time acceleration of fatigue life estimation. Ref. [23] applied
intelligent learning methods to the active power regulation of wind turbines, considering
both power command tracking and fatigue mitigation of the main shaft and tower. The
aforementioned research demonstrates that machine learning techniques are capable of
accurately capturing the nonlinear mapping relationships between variables such as wind
speed, operating status, and fatigue loads. By serving as approximate surrogates for high-
fidelity simulations, these approaches provide a robust and efficient tool for the rapid
prediction of fatigue loads under complex operating scenarios.
However, most existing machine learning load surrogate models focus on power
optimization and fatigue load assessment [24,25], whereas few studies have considered the
direct influence of frequency-regulation control parameters on fatigue loads. In primary
frequency response scenarios, these control parameters directly determine the intensity
of frequency support, the power regulation process, and the resulting additional load
levels. Therefore, surrogate models established under normal operating conditions are
difficult to apply directly to rapid fatigue assessment under frequency-regulation conditions.
Moreover, when the scope of analysis expands from individual turbines to the wind-farm
level, the challenge is no longer limited to the rapid estimation of fatigue loads for a
single turbine, but also involves integrating single-turbine fatigue-response assessment
into

2.1 Wind Turbine Model
sections.text:
A wind turbine is a system that converts wind energy into mechanical energy through
its mechanical structure and subsequently into electrical energy via a generator. It typically
consists of an aerodynamic subsystem, drivetrain, pitch control system, electrical system,
control subsystem, and tower.
The aerodynamic subsystem captures wind energy and mainly comprises the blades
and hub, collectively referred to as the rotor. As wind passes through the rotor, it is
decelerated, and part of its kinetic energy is converted into mechanical energy. In theoretical
analysis, the key physical quantities used to describe the aerodynamic characteristics of
a wind turbine are the mechanical power Pm and the aerodynamic thrust Ft which are
expressed in Equations (1) and (2), respectively [26].

pitch angle, v is the incoming wind speed, λ is the tip speed ratio defined as λ = ωrR/v,
ωr is the rotor speed and Ct is the thrust coefficient of the wind turbine.
In fatigue analysis of the tower structure, the fatigue load at the tower base is typically
used as a representative indicator of the overall structural fatigue load.
Therefore, the bending moment at the tower base is adopted as a key indicator to
evaluate tower fatigue loads [27], as expressed in Equation (3).

where Ht is the height of the wind turbine tower.
The drivetrain is a critical mechanical structure that connects the aerodynamic system
and the electrical system of a wind turbine, and its primary function is to transmit the
mechanical energy captured by the rotor from the airflow to the generator via the main
shaft and gearbox, enabling the conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy.
In the fatigue load analysis of wind turbines, in order to more accurately describe the
dynamic characteristics of the drivetrain, a two-mass model is adopted to represent the

sections.text:
During system power disturbances, wind turbines contribute to frequency regulation
via virtual inertia and droop control strategies [ 8]. Virtual inertia control enables rapid
release of turbine kinetic energy in the early stage of frequency variation, improving the
system’s inertial response capability. Droop control provides stable power support during
the sustained frequency deviation stage. The corresponding power regulation amount ∆P

sections.title: 3 Fatigue Load Data Acquisition and MLP Prediction Model
3.1 Fatigue Load Evaluation
sections.text:
In the below-rated wind speed region, wind turbines can participate in grid frequency
regulation via coordinated virtual inertia control. Virtual inertia control primarily responds
to the rate of change of frequency, whereas droop control responds to frequency devia-
tion; their combined action enables rapid active power adjustment over short time scales.
However, such power regulation induces dynamic variations in generator electromagnetic
torque, drivetrain torque, and tower aerodynamic thrust, thereby modifying the load-cycle
characteristics of critical structural components, including the main shaft and tower. Since
fatigue damage is primarily determined by the amplitude and frequency distribution of
load cycles, the participation of wind turbines in frequency regulation can significantly
influence the process of structural fatigue accumulation.
To quantify this effect, the rainflow counting method is first employed to decompose
the load time series into individual load cycles. This method identifies equivalent cycles
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16094476
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 4476 6 of 31
from irregular variable-amplitude load histories and determines the amplitude and number
of occurrences of each cycle, thus providing the basis for subsequent fatigue damage
assessment. The material S–N curve is then used to establish the relationship between
load amplitude and fatigue life, which describes the number of cycles that the material
can withstand under a given stress or load level [28]. On this basis, Miner’s linear damage
accumulation rule is adopted to calculate the cumulative fatigue damage caused by load
cycles with different amplitudes, thereby obtaining the total fatigue damage over the
reference period. Finally, the accumulated damage is converted into the damage equivalent
load (DEL), which is used to characterize the fatigue effect of loads on critical structural
components of wind turbines. The 1 Hz DEL corresponding to the reference period Tref is
calculated as follows:
DEL = (∑
NiSm

Si is the load amplitude of the i-th cycle obtained from rainflow counting, m is the slope ex-
ponent of the material S–N curve in logarithmic coordinates which depends on the material
properties of the structural component and Nre f is the reference number of cycles, typically
taken as the equivalent number of cycles over the design lifetime of the wind turbine.
In this study, the tower base fore–aft bending moment, tower base side-to-side bending
moment, and rotor torque are selected as the primary fatigue load channels. The selection
is motivated by the fact that the tower base fore–aft and side-to-side bending moments
represent the loading characteristics of the tower in different directions, whereas the rotor
torque captures load variations in the drivetrain; these variables correspond to the tower
and drivetrain, which are the critical structural components most significantly influenced
by frequency regulation control [ 11,29]. In contrast, blade loads are more sensitive to
stochastic wind speed fluctuations and exhibit relatively weak responses to changes in
control parameters under the primary frequency regulation scenarios considered in this
study [30]. Therefore, the above three load channels are selected for fatigue analysis, and

sections.text:
OpenFAST is a modular, open-source wind turbine dynamics simulation tool devel-
oped by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), which has been certified by
Germanischer Lloyd (GL) and can accurately simulate the dynamic response of both rigid
and flexible mechanical structures of wind turbines [31].
To comprehensively simulate the frequency response of wind turbines in power system
frequency regulation, while accounting for mechanical structural dynamics and enabling
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16094476

OpenFAST and Matlab/Simulink (v2025a). The turbine mechanical dynamics are modeled
in OpenFAST, whereas the wind turbine control system [ 32] and a fast grid simulation
model (GSFR) based on the IEEE 9-bus system are developed in Matlab/Simulink, and deep
integration between OpenFAST and Simulink is realized through an S-Function interface.
The IEEE 9-bus system considered has a total load of 692 MW. The detailed co-simulation

To investigate the influence of coordinated virtual inertia control on the mechanical

From a structural response perspective, the additional power introduced by frequency
regulation leads to an imbalance between mechanical torque and electromagnetic torque,
thereby exacerbating fluctuations in drivetrain torque and tower bending moments. In
other words, higher values of Kd f and Kp f are associated with an increase in the overall
DEL of the wind turbine, indicating a positive correlation between the control gains and
structural fatigue load. Therefore, there exists an inherent trade-off between improved
frequency regulation capability and increased structural fatigue. The key objective of
this study is to, while satisfying frequency regulation requirements, effectively reduce
the overall fatigue load of the wind farm and significantly improve the balance of load
distribution among turbines, thereby avoiding the concentration of frequency regulation

burden on a small number of units, which could compromise the overall lifespan of the
wind farm.

sections.title: 3.3 Wind Turbine Damage Equivalent Load Characteristic Database
sections.text:
Based on the theoretical calculation of DEL, the fluctuation of the main shaft torque
originates from variations in wind resources and active power output. The fluctuation
of the tower base bending moment is mainly related to the aerodynamic thrust acting on
the turbine. Based on the above analysis, this study selects power disturbance magnitude,
wind speed, virtual inertia coefficient, and droop coefficient as the fundamental operating
parameters to characterize the DEL of the drivetrain and tower.
To ensure that the constructed sample scenarios have a clear system background
and engineering representativeness, the selection of parameter ranges for the frequency
regulation conditions in this paper is not arbitrarily set based on experience. Instead,
it is determined based on the established IEEE 9-bus system model [ 34]. This system
is composed of thermal power units, hydropower units, and a wind farm, which can
reflect the typical frequency dynamic characteristics under the coexistence of traditional
synchronous units and wind farms. Therefore, the representativeness of the operating
scenarios discussed in this paper primarily targets the typical operation of wind farms
participating in primary frequency regulation within such hybrid thermal–hydro–wind
power systems.
The wind speed data samples used in this study were obtained from a real wind farm
(hereinafter referred to as the LY wind farm), which consists of 48 DFIG units. The power
output and wind speed data of all turbines in the LY wind farm for the entire year of 2015
were collected; however, because the cut-in wind speed of the DFIG model was 5 m/s, only
data corresponding to wind speeds above 5 m/s were retained, with a sampling interval
of 10 min. Since the original wind speed data were sampled at a minute-level time scale,
whereas primary frequency regulation occurs on a second-level time scale, there exists a
significant temporal mismatch between the two. On the second-level time scale, wind speed
varies relatively slowly and can therefore be assumed constant during a single frequency
regulation event. Based on this, a constant wind speed assumption was adopted when
constructing individual frequency regulation samples, whereby the wind speed of each
turbine within the corresponding time period was treated as a constant input parameter.
During the sample construction process, the range of power disturbance magnitudes
is determined based on the frequency response results under the IEEE 9-bus system SFR
model in this paper. Specifically, by analyzing the response law of the frequency nadir
varying with disturbances, this paper selects a power disturbance interval that covers
different levels of frequency support demand. This represents typical scenarios of wind
farm participation in primary frequency regulation under varying disturbance intensities.
On this basis, the power disturbance ranges from 0.0283 to 0.1133 with a step size of 0.0094.
The wind speed ranges from 7 to 11 m/s with a step size of 0.5 m/s. Both the virtual inertia
coefficient and droop coefficient range from 0 to 100 with a step size of 10. A total of 9801
frequency regulation scenarios are generated based on these parameter combinations.
In the co-simulation model, operating conditions with a simulation duration of 200 s
were generated, and the load time series of two key components—the tower and drivetrain—
under frequency support were obtained using OpenFAST. The DEL over this period was
then calculated via rainflow counting, thereby establishing a DEL database for wind
turbines during frequency regulation.

sections.title: 3.4 MLP Neural Network Prediction Model
sections.text:
Due to the complex nonlinear mapping among frequency regulation variables, op-
erating conditions, and fatigue loads, as well as the high computational cost associated
with directly using high-fidelity co-simulation for DEL evaluation during optimization,
this study employed a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network to construct a fast
DEL prediction model. The MLP is a typical feedforward neural network with strong
nonlinear function approximation capability and can learn complex mappings between
input variables and output responses through multiple hidden layers, making it suitable
for fast regression modeling of the relationship between frequency regulation variables
and fatigue load indicators of wind turbines [ 35]. In this study, the power disturbance
magnitude, wind speed, virtual inertia coefficient, and droop coefficient in the sample
database were used as inputs to the neural network, while the DEL values corresponding to
the tower fore–aft bending moment, tower side-to-side bending moment, and rotor torque
were used as outputs, enabling rapid prediction of key fatigue loads under frequency
regulation conditions.
The prediction performance of the MLP neural network is relatively sensitive to
hyperparameters such as the hidden layer structure, activation function, learning rate,
regularization coefficient, and batch size. To reduce the empiricism in the hyperparameter
selection process, this paper uses the grid search combined with 5-fold cross-validation
method to optimize the key hyperparameters of the model. Specifically, different parameter
combinations are trained and validated individually within the predefined search space,
and the coefficient of determination (R2) under 5-fold cross-validation is used as the pri-
mary evaluation metric to select the parameter configuration with the best comprehensive
performance. Table 3 MLP model hyperparameter search space and optimal results. shows
the hyperparameter search space and optimal results of the MLP model. The hyperpa-
rameter search results show that when the hidden layer structure is (64, 32), the activation
function is ReLU, the learning rate is 0.001, the regularization coefficient is 0.001, and the
batch size is 64, the model achieves a good balance among prediction accuracy, training
stability, and complexity. Therefore, the subsequent model training and testing in this paper
are all based on this optimal parameter configuration.
Table 3. MLP model hyperparameter search space and optimal results.

The training and inference of the MLP model are implemented based on the PyTorch
platform, and the samples are divided into training and testing sets at a ratio of 80% to 20%.
Meanwhile, the input and output data are standardized, and an early stopping mechanism
is introduced to improve the stability of model training. To reduce the risk of model
overfitting, a Dropout mechanism is introduced in the hidden layers. The ReLU activation
function is employed to bolster the network’s nonlinear approximation capabilities. Finally,
the Mean Squared Error (MSE) is adopted as the loss function, and the model is optimized
utilizing the Adam optimizer.

sections.title: 4 Wind Farm Control Parameter Optimization Strategy
4.1 Problem Description of Optimization
sections.text:
To resolve the trade-off between frequency support demands and fatigue load increase
in wind farm primary frequency regulation, the virtual inertia and droop coefficients of
each turbine were selected as decision variables, and a control parameter selective reduction
optimization model incorporating system frequency security constraints was developed.
This section formulates the problem from three perspectives—decision variables, objec-
tive function, and constraints—thereby providing a formal problem definition for the
subsequent rolling optimization strategy.
For a wind farm consisting of 48 turbines, each turbine is assigned independent virtual
inertia and droop coefficients, resulting in a total of 96 optimization variables, which can
be expressed as:
X = [Kd f,1, Kp f,1, . . . ,Kd f,N, Kp f,N] (19)
where N = 48 denotes the number of wind turbines in the wind farm.
To simultaneously reduce overall fatigue load and improve load distribution uni-
formity among turbines, a composite objective function centered on total DEL and DEL
variance is formulated. Specifically, total DEL characterizes the aggregate fatigue load of
the wind farm, whereas DEL variance measures the dispersion of fatigue load distribution
